strengths: Identifies and formalizes a practically important and underexplored problem setting combining three real-world challenges simultaneously: channel-wise asynchronous sampling periods, block-wise test-time missingness, and inter-channel dependency, motivated with concrete industrial examples.

Provides a clear theoretical/analytical explanation (Appendix B) of why linear interpolation introduces spectral distortion (amplitude attenuation, spectral leakage, phase delay), which nicely supports the design choice of avoiding interpolation.

Extensive empirical evaluation across three modified public benchmarks and one real-world industrial (LNG carrier) dataset, with multiple architecturally diverse baselines (Transformer, CNN, GNN, MLP-based).

Thorough ablation studies: component-wise ablation (dependency/asynchrony/missingness), six variants of attention masking strategy, number of channel tokens, robustness to varying test-time input lengths, and frequency-domain fidelity analysis.
Also validates the model in the conventional (fully-observed, synchronously sampled) forecasting setting, showing it remains competitive there, which strengthens the generality claim.
Reports error bars over multiple seeds for main results, improving credibility of comparisons.
weaknesses: The 'asynchronous' benchmark datasets are synthetically constructed by downsampling originally synchronous data (ETTm1, Weather, Monash), so it's unclear whether this fully captures the complexities of genuinely asynchronous real-world sensor networks; results on the single real industrial dataset (CHS) are less extensively analyzed and not clearly available for reproducibility.

Performance improvements over strong baselines (e.g., TimeXer, PatchTST) are often modest (roughly 3-10%), and given the reported error bars, some gains may be only marginally significant in certain settings/datasets.

Despite extensively discussing the irregular/asynchronous time series literature in Related Work, the paper does not empirically compare against any of these dedicated irregular-sampling methods (e.g., ContiFormer, Raindrop, GraFITi-style models), which would be a natural and more direct baseline category for the asynchronous setting, rather than only comparing to standard synchronous forecasters fed interpolated data.

The core architectural novelty is somewhat incremental, combining known ideas (global/CLS-like summary tokens, patch dropout/masking, frequency-informed patch length selection, read-only attention masking) into a new configuration rather than introducing fundamentally new mechanisms.

The authors acknowledge a genuine scalability limitation (quadratic attention cost growing with channel count) but provide no empirical runtime/memory/parameter-count comparison against baselines to quantify this trade-off.
No mention of code or the real-world CHS dataset release, limiting reproducibility, particularly since baseline reimplementations (e.g., CrossGNN) and custom dataset constructions are involved.
The number of channel tokens and masking strategy appear to require per-dataset tuning (Table 4, Table 10), suggesting sensitivity to hyperparameters that may complicate deployment in new settings.

strengths: Addresses a practically motivated and underexplored combination of problems: channel-wise asynchronous sampling periods, block-wise test-time missingness, and inter-channel dependency, which is a reasonable gap to target.

The architectural idea of channel tokens as compressed, variable-length-agnostic summaries that mediate cross-channel attention while local tokens handle intra-channel temporal modeling is a sensible and relatively clean design.

Extensive ablations are provided (channel dependence, dynamic patching, patch masking, number of channel tokens, six variants of attention masking strategies, input-length robustness), which helps isolate the contribution of individual components.
Inclusion of a real-world industrial dataset (LNG Cargo Handling System) in addition to three modified public benchmarks adds some practical grounding.

The theoretical discussion of interpolation-induced spectral distortion (Appendix B) is a nice, if somewhat standard, signal-processing explanation for why interpolation-based baselines may underperform.
weaknesses: Although missingness handling is advertised as one of the three core contributions, and the related-work section explicitly discusses BRITS, GRU-D, RAINDROP, and SERT as missing-data-aware methods, none of these are included as baselines; only generic forecasting models (interpolated/zero-filled) are compared, making the claimed advantage under missingness largely untested against appropriate competitors.

The 'practical' datasets are constructed by artificially downsampling channels of originally uniformly-sampled benchmarks (ETTm1, Weather, Monash Solar/Wind) to different fixed periods. Because the 'ground truth' at coarse resolution is just a subsample of the same finely-sampled series used to derive CTF's non-interpolated inputs, the experimental setup may structurally favor an interpolation-free approach and does not necessarily reflect genuine asynchronous real-world sensor behavior (independent noise, drift, heterogeneous underlying processes).

Reported performance gains over strong baselines (TimeXer, PatchTST, iTransformer, TimeMixer) are often small in absolute terms (e.g., CMSE differences of 0.01-0.03), and per-length error bars (Table 13/14) frequently overlap between CTF and the best baseline, raising doubts about the statistical/practical significance of the claimed 'consistent' superiority.

The frequency-domain fidelity analysis (Section 6.3, Table 6) shows essentially negligible differences between CTF and TimeXer (e.g., dominant frequency difference 0.0098 vs 0.0099), which weakens the claimed support for the interpolation-free argument despite being presented as a key piece of evidence.

The number of channel tokens is dataset-specific and manually tuned (1, 2, or 3), with no principled selection rule beyond post-hoc rationalization, suggesting limited robustness/generalizability of the architecture across domains.

The model's own stated limitation—quadratic attention cost growing with number of channels—undermines applicability to realistic high-dimensional sensor systems; this is acknowledged but not addressed, and the CHS dataset experiment already subsamples only 10 of 52 available channels, sidestepping the scalability question the paper itself raises.
No computational cost/runtime/parameter-count comparison with baselines is provided, despite claims of 'parameter efficiency' from the unified attention design.

The CHS real-world dataset, which is the strongest evidence of practical relevance, is proprietary, has limited methodological detail, and is not released, hurting reproducibility; no code/data release is mentioned anywhere in the paper.

The paper text is long and repetitive in motivating the problem (introduction and related work restate the same asynchrony/missingness motivation multiple times) while the core methodological novelty (masked unified attention with channel tokens) is a relatively incremental combination of existing ideas (read-only prompt attention, patch-based tokenization, random patch masking akin to patch dropout).

strengths: Tackles a genuinely practical and underexplored triad of challenges in multivariate forecasting (channel dependency, asynchronous sampling, block-wise test-time missingness) rather than a single isolated problem, and provides a clear unifying formulation (CMSE/CMAE over channel-specific horizons).

The architectural design is well-motivated and reasonably novel: frequency-adaptive dynamic patching avoids forcing all channels onto a common grid, and the unified masked-attention scheme elegantly merges intra-channel temporal modeling with inter-channel dependency modeling using channel tokens as compressed, variable-length-agnostic summaries.

Extensive empirical evaluation: three modified benchmark datasets plus one real industrial dataset (LNG cargo handling system), multiple missingness ratios, and a conventional (non-asynchronous) forecasting setting showing the model is still competitive there.

Thorough ablation studies, including component-wise ablations (dependency/asynchrony/missingness), six variants of attention masking strategies, sensitivity to number of channel tokens, and robustness to variable test-time input lengths.

Good supplementary theoretical analysis (Appendix B) explaining why linear interpolation induces amplitude attenuation, spectral leakage, and phase delay, which supports the motivation for an interpolation-free design and is corroborated by the frequency-domain comparison against TimeXer.
Reports error bars over 5 random seeds for the main asynchronous/missingness experiments, improving confidence in the reported gains.
weaknesses: The three 'practical' benchmark datasets (ETT1, Weather, SolarWind) are synthetically constructed by manually assigning sampling periods to channels of existing benchmarks, which may not faithfully capture the statistical properties of truly asynchronous real-world sensor networks; only one dataset (CHS) is genuinely real-world and asynchronous, limiting the strength of the generalization claims.

Despite extensive discussion of irregularly-sampled time series literature (mTAN, GRU-D, RAINDROP, ContiFormer, IMTS-Mixer, etc.) in Related Work, none of these methods are included as baselines, even though they are directly relevant to handling missingness and non-uniform sampling; comparisons are limited to standard MTS forecasters run on interpolated inputs, which is a somewhat weaker baseline treatment for the missingness setting.

Gains over the strongest baselines are often modest (e.g., a few percent CMSE improvement in Table 1 for ETT1/SolarWind), and in the conventional (non-practical) multivariate setting (Table 11) CTF is not consistently the best model (e.g., SimpleTM outperforms on ETTh2), suggesting the method's advantage is somewhat setting-specific rather than a universal improvement.

The block-wise missing-value evaluation protocol (blocks sized exactly to one patch length in SolarWind) appears tailored to align with the model's own patch-masking mechanism, which could bias the comparison in the model's favor relative to baselines that were not designed with this granularity in mind.

Scalability is an acknowledged but unaddressed limitation: the unified attention layer scales quadratically with the number of local+channel tokens, and experiments use datasets with a limited number of channels (up to ~21, with only 10 selected from 52 in CHS), leaving open how the method performs on higher-dimensional real-world systems.

The paper's presentation is dense with many design choices and hyperparameters (patch length selection via FFT dominant frequency, number of channel tokens, masking variants) that are tuned per-dataset, raising some concern about reproducibility and practical applicability without extensive per-dataset tuning.

strengths: Addresses a well-motivated and underexplored combination of three practical challenges simultaneously (channel dependency, asynchronous sampling, and missingness), rather than treating them in isolation as most prior work does.

Extensive empirical evaluation across six datasets (four adapted benchmarks, one industrial LNG dataset, one air-quality dataset), covering two case studies (asynchrony-only and asynchrony+missingness), with consistent improvements over a wide range of baselines spanning Transformer, CNN/MLP/GNN, and irregular-time-series architectures.

Thorough ablation studies isolating the contribution of channel dependence, dynamic patching, and patch masking, plus additional ablations on channel embeddings, patch length choices, and six attention-masking variants.

Good supporting analyses beyond raw accuracy numbers: frequency-domain analysis quantifying interpolation-induced spectral distortion (theoretically and empirically), scalability analysis (channel count and input length), and robustness to input-length variability at test time.
Reasonable reproducibility effort: detailed hyperparameters, dataset construction procedures, error bars over multiple seeds, and an explicit reproducibility/ethics statement.
weaknesses: Core architectural ingredients (channel-level summary tokens, frequency-guided variable-length patching, random patch/token dropout as a masking strategy, read-only attention masks) are each drawn fairly directly from existing works (iTransformer/TimeXer, Moirai/LightGTS, PatchDropout, read-only prompt attention); the paper's contribution is primarily their combination and adaptation, which is somewhat incremental rather than conceptually novel.

Reported performance gains over the strongest baseline (TimeXer) are often small in absolute terms (frequently 0.01-0.03 CMSE/CMAE), raising questions about the practical significance of the improvement relative to the added architectural complexity (extra channel tokens, custom attention masks, frequency-based patch length search).

Most 'practical' asynchronous datasets (ETT1/ETT2, Weather, SolarWind) are synthetically constructed by resampling standard benchmarks with manually assigned per-channel sampling periods, rather than being genuinely irregular real-world data; only EPA and the private CHS dataset reflect truly heterogeneous real sampling, somewhat weakening the 'real-world' framing.

The optimal number of channel tokens (1-3) is dataset-dependent and must be tuned per dataset (Table 4), reducing the plug-and-play nature of the method and adding another hyperparameter to search compared to simpler baselines.

Several irregular-time-series baselines (ContiFormer, t-PatchGNN, Hi-Patch, CrossGNN, BiTGraph) were reimplemented/integrated into a different (TimesNet-based) codebase than their original release, which could introduce implementation discrepancies that affect the fairness of comparison, and ContiFormer's ODE solver was approximated for efficiency, potentially altering its true behavior.

Scalability analysis shows OOM at 280 channels on a 24GB GPU and quadratic growth in runtime/memory with channel count, which could limit applicability to larger real-world sensor networks (e.g., industrial systems with hundreds of channels), a point the paper acknowledges as future work.

strengths: Tackles a genuinely underexplored combination of practical challenges (channel-wise asynchronous sampling, block-wise test-time missingness, and cross-channel dependency) that most prior forecasting work addresses only in isolation.

Extensive experimental coverage across multiple modified public benchmarks and one private industrial dataset, plus a wide range of baseline categories (CD/CI Transformers, CNN/GNN/MLP, irregular-sampling and missingness-aware models).

Reasonably thorough ablation studies (component removal, masking-strategy variants, channel-token count, input-length robustness) and a scalability analysis showing where the architecture breaks down (OOM at ~280 channels).
The frequency-domain analysis of interpolation-induced distortion (amplitude attenuation, spectral leakage, phase delay) is a nice theoretical framing that motivates the interpolation-free design.
Error bars over multiple seeds are reported in the appendix, which is good practice for reproducibility.
weaknesses: The core architectural novelty is limited: the paper explicitly acknowledges its channel-token idea 'resembles' iTransformer/TimeXer summary tokens, and the frequency-guided dynamic patching and PatchDropout-based masking are directly repurposed from prior univariate/vision works rather than newly developed for this setting; the contribution reads largely as an engineering integration of existing components under a unifying mask.

Reported gains over the strongest baselines are frequently marginal (e.g., ETT2: 0.377 vs 0.380 CMSE; ETT1: 0.399 vs 0.411; CHS CMAE ties with tPatchGNN) and often fall within one standard deviation shown in the appendix tables, raising doubts about the practical significance of the improvements.

The 'practical' asynchronous benchmarks are all synthetically constructed by resampling standard datasets (ETTm1/2, Weather, Monash Solar/Wind) according to the authors' own heuristics, rather than being genuinely irregular real-world data; this raises concern that the benchmark setup was designed to favor the proposed model rather than reflecting an externally validated notion of real-world asynchrony.

The evaluation protocol embeds an architectural advantage into the problem setup itself: regular baselines are forced through lossy linear interpolation while CTF operates interpolation-free by design, so part of the reported gap reflects the preprocessing choice rather than a controlled comparison of model capacity; even the 'interpolation-free' modified TimeXer variant only partially closes this gap, suggesting the benefit is more from problem framing than from the proposed attention mechanism.

Several irregular/missingness baselines (ContiFormer, Hi-Patch, t-PatchGNN, BiTGraph, CrossGNN) were reimplemented into the TimesNet framework rather than run with their original codebases, which could introduce implementation discrepancies that are hard to verify and may understate their true performance.

The optimal number of channel tokens (1, 2, or 3) must be tuned per dataset without a principled selection rule; the post-hoc explanation based on 'channel similarity and diversity' is speculative and not independently validated.

Ablation results show some components contribute very little in certain regimes (e.g., 'w/o patch masking' only changes CMSE from 0.452 to 0.458 at m=0.375), weakening the claim that all three components are strictly necessary in a strong, consistent sense.
The private CHS dataset limits reproducibility, and code availability is only promised 'upon publication' rather than provided for review.

Standard MSE-based loss and CMSE metric are used throughout despite the paper's own discussion (Section G) acknowledging that MSE fails to penalize amplitude attenuation/over-smoothing, meaning the paper's own evaluation may not fully capture the qualitative advantages it claims (e.g., spectral fidelity) in the main quantitative tables.

Scalability analysis reveals real limits (OOM at 280 channels, quadratic attention cost) that could constrain applicability to larger real-world industrial systems, which somewhat undercuts the 'real-world' framing emphasized in the title.

strengths: Addresses a well-motivated, practically important, and underexplored combination of three challenges (channel-wise asynchronous sampling, block-wise test-time missingness, and cross-channel dependency) that prior work has only tackled in isolation.

The proposed mask-guided unified attention over local and channel tokens is a clean architectural mechanism that avoids interpolation, unifies intra/inter-channel modeling in a single attention operation, and naturally accommodates variable patch counts per channel.

Extensive empirical evaluation: six datasets (four adapted public benchmarks, one real industrial LNG dataset, one EPA air-quality dataset), multiple experimental cases (asynchrony alone, asynchrony+missingness at varying ratios), and results reported with error bars over multiple seeds.

Thorough ablation studies isolating the contribution of channel dependence, dynamic patching, and patch masking, as well as an ablation over six different attention masking strategy variants and the number of channel tokens.

Useful supplementary analyses: theoretical/empirical frequency-domain explanation of interpolation-induced distortion, scalability analysis (channel count and input length) showing practical feasibility, and robustness to variable input length at test time without retraining.
Also validates the model in the conventional (non-asynchronous, fully observed) setting, showing it remains competitive with SOTA baselines there, not just in the newly proposed practical setting.
Good reproducibility and ethics documentation, and reasonable baseline coverage spanning channel-dependent, channel-independent, irregular-sampling, and missingness-aware methods.
weaknesses: Performance gains over the strongest baselines (e.g., TimeXer, PatchTST) are often modest on several datasets (e.g., ETT2, Weather, SolarWind in Case 1), raising questions about the practical significance of the improvement despite the added architectural complexity.

Four of the six evaluation datasets are synthetically constructed by artificially resampling channels of standard benchmarks (ETTm1/ETTm2, Weather) to simulate asynchrony; while reasonable, this raises some concern about how well these mimic true real-world sampling heterogeneity versus the two genuinely real datasets (EPA, CHS).

The core architectural novelty (channel tokens acting as compact per-channel summaries with cross-channel attention) builds directly on iTransformer/TimeXer with an added masking scheme, making the technical contribution somewhat incremental relative to prior channel-token-based transformers.

Several design choices (e.g., 70th-percentile FFT threshold for dominant frequency detection, fallback patching heuristics, choice of number of channel tokens per dataset) appear empirically tuned without strong theoretical justification or systematic sensitivity analysis beyond a coarse ablation.

The self-attention mechanism scales quadratically with the number of local+channel tokens; scalability analysis shows OOM around 280 channels on a single 24GB GPU, which may be limiting for larger real-world industrial systems with hundreds of sensors.

The custom CMSE/CMAE metrics, while justified by heterogeneous per-channel horizons, complicate direct comparison with numbers reported in other papers on the same base datasets (e.g., standard ETTm1/Weather results), and the practical-setting datasets are not established as a standard shared benchmark.
The private CHS dataset limits full reproducibility of one of the real-world validation results.

The frequency-bias analysis (Section 6.3) is limited to a single dataset/prediction length and a single baseline comparison (TimeXer), providing only weak support for the broader claim about interpolation-induced spectral distortion mitigation.
